patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2003: Keating Report — Situation of Children in the Care of the Jamaican State (2003).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Jamaica — Keating Report on children in state care finds sexual abuse by caregivers (2003); Jamaica — child sex trafficking in resort towns; 6.3% of 12–17-year-olds (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Sri Lankan peacekeepers in Haiti (MINUSTAH) (2007): None convicted by Sri Lanka; one-off ex gratia payment to one victim (2016)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 1987: ban: Sri Lanka imposes temporary ban on foreign adoptions after baby-farm raid (20 newborns, 22 women found) 2017: scandal: Zembla documentary; Sri Lanka's health minister admits 1980s 'baby farms' and announces inquiry (September) 2020: acknowledgment: Swiss Federal Council acknowledges authorities' irregularities in Sri Lankan adoptions (also 2023) 2021: suspension: Netherlands suspension covers adoptions from all countries incl. Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil, Colombia
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Home country of accused troops or staff
patterns.role_note: Sri Lanka → Haiti: MINUSTAH contingent (offenders).
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
cases.who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
cases.what: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.
cases.cover_up: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Norway — NOU 2026:7 finds illegal and unethical intercountry adoptions
cases.who: Norwegian adoption organisations; Norwegian authorities; partner orphanages and bodies in 12 countries
cases.what: A government committee appointed in 2023 presented NOU 2026:7 'Forsvarlighet, risiko og tillit' on 22 June 2026. Examining adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s, it concluded there were illegal or unethical conditions and that the Norwegian adoption system had clear shortcomings throughout the period. Individual findings included a kidnapped child adopted to Norway, a mother told she would get money if she consented, and documents deliberately falsified; payments to orphanages or organisations were sometimes linked to the number of children adopted.
cases.cover_up: Organisations did not always tell Norwegian authorities about payments or errors; authorities kept approving adoptions after learning of risks and illegalities.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Seth Sevana children's home, Vavuniya — monk arrested, bail with NCPA consent
cases.who: Seth Sevana Lama Nivasa children's home (run by a Buddhist monk) housing war-affected Tamil children; National Child Protection Authority (NCPA)
cases.what: In October 2013 the head of a children's home in Vavuniya, a Buddhist monk, was arrested for sexually abusing a 9-year-old child, confirmed by medical evidence on 12 October 2013. The NCPA took custody of the other 22 children on 15 October 2013. Most children were war-affected Tamil children placed by poor families. Groundviews reported that complaints had reached the NCPA since 2010 and that the agency later supported his release on bail.
cases.cover_up: Complaints had been made to the NCPA since 2010; the arrest came only after protests by Vavuniya child protection officers. On 31 December 2013 the monk got unconditional bail after the Attorney General's Department, on NCPA instructions, told the court it had no objection; the NCPA did not submit the 22 children's reports to the court.

cases.who: Foreign and local offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers reportedly exploit boys and girls in child sex trafficking, including in coastal areas, for foreign offenders, and recommends investigating complicit establishments. The government convicted six traffickers and identified seven child victims in the year.

patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role: Offenders' home country: law to prosecute abroad
patterns.role_note: 2013: Terre des Hommes "Sweetie" sting: 20,000 internet users in 10 weeks offered to pay for webcam sex with an apparent Filipino child; of 21,000 perpetrators, 1,000 were identified (from Australia, Canada, Germany, India, the Netherlands, the UK, the US and others), incl. 110 in the UK and 254 in the US — early evidence of "webcam child sex tourism"
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 33,788 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (11% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended; De Winter Commission — violence in Dutch youth care since 1945.
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Amsterdam daycare abuse case (Het Hofnarretje) and the Gunning commission
cases.who: Robert Mikelsons (childcare worker at Het Hofnarretje and Jenno's Knuffelparadijs) and his partner Richard van O.
cases.what: Childcare worker Robert Mikelsons abused babies and toddlers at two Amsterdam daycare centres and as a babysitter between February 2007 and January 2010. On 21 May 2012 the Amsterdam district court sentenced him to 18 years plus compulsory psychiatric detention (TBS); he was charged over 67 children and admitted abusing 87, and the appeal court raised the sentence to 19 years on 26 April 2013. His partner Richard van O. was sentenced to six years as an accessory. On 15 April 2011 a commission chaired by Louise Gunning-Schepers found that daycare centres, government bodies and others had failed, that risk signals were missed, and that a 2008 anonymous report had not been acted on.
cases.cover_up: An anonymous tip to Meld Misdaad Anoniem in 2008 was not acted on; the Gunning commission called it a missed opportunity.

cases.title: Special Court for Sierra Leone — Charles Taylor convicted of aiding sexual slavery and use of child soldiers (2012)
cases.who: Charles Taylor, former President of Liberia; Revolutionary United Front (RUF) and allied rebel forces he aided
cases.what: On 26 April 2012 the Special Court for Sierra Leone, sitting in The Hague, convicted former Liberian president Charles Taylor on all 11 counts of war crimes and crimes against humanity, on the basis of aiding and abetting crimes by the Revolutionary United Front during Sierra Leone's civil war, including sexual slavery and the recruitment and use of children under 15 as fighters. He was sentenced to 50 years in prison in May 2012.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Operation Torpedo — FBI ran three Tor sites
cases.who: Three Tor-hidden abuse sites run by a Nebraska man
cases.what: Dutch police compromised one site and found it physically hosted at a Nebraska web host; the FBI found an employee running two sites at work and one at home. After a year of surveillance the FBI arrested him and operated the sites for two weeks, using a network investigative technique to reveal visitors' IP addresses. The US DOJ said in December 2015 that 18 US users had been convicted besides the operator; one was the acting cybersecurity director of the US Department of Health and Human Services.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: Peter Scully — pay-per-view abuse streamed from Mindanao
cases.who: 'No Limits Fun' dark web site (Peter Scully, Australian; Filipino accomplices)
cases.what: An Australian from Melbourne who moved to Cagayan de Oro, Mindanao, in 2011 was alleged to have run a ring that abused children and sold videos of the abuse online to customers abroad. The Philippine investigation began with a tip from Dutch police, who found images on a seized hard drive. Arrested in 2015, he was charged with the murder of a 12-year-old girl as well as trafficking and child abuse. In June 2018 a Cagayan de Oro court sentenced him to life imprisonment after convicting him of one count of human trafficking and five counts of rape. On 3 November 2022, under a plea bargain, he was sentenced to a further 129 years; his former girlfriend, a co-accused, got 126 years and two others more than nine years each.

cases.title: Netherlands — National Rapporteur estimate of exploited Dutch girls
cases.who: Domestic pimps and 'loverboy' recruiters
cases.what: A report by National Rapporteur Corinne Dettmeijer, prepared with UNODC and published 18 October 2017, estimated that at least 1,320 underage Dutch girls aged 12 to 17 fall victim to sexual exploitation in the Netherlands each year, using 2012–2016 data. Underage girls made up nearly half of female victims in the Dutch sex industry. In October 2025 the current rapporteur reported reported exploitation cases rising from 868 (2023) to 944 (2024), with more teenage victims.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: Samson Commission — sexual abuse of children in Dutch state care
cases.who: Dutch children's homes and foster care (Jeugdzorg)
cases.what: The commission chaired by former procurator-general Rieke Samson reported in October 2012 on sexual abuse of children in state-arranged care since 1945. It received 800 claims, 65% about children's homes and 30% about foster families, and passed 42 files to the public prosecutor. It found the government, care homes and foster care services did not do enough to protect children and, once aware, lacked professionalism and courage to act.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Netherlands — Joustra committee: state failed to stop intercountry adoption abuses; all adoptions suspended
cases.who: Dutch government (Justice ministry), licensed Dutch adoption intermediaries, intermediaries in sending countries
cases.what: The Commission of Inquiry into Intercountry Adoption, set up in 2019 and chaired by Tjibbe Joustra, reported in February 2021 after a two-year investigation that found 'serious violations' in adoptions from countries including Sri Lanka, Indonesia, Bangladesh, Brazil and Colombia between 1967 and 1997/98, and concluded the Dutch government had for decades failed to prevent abuses and protect children's rights. The government suspended all intercountry adoptions with immediate effect on 8 February 2021. About 4,000 of the children were from Sri Lanka.
cases.cover_up: The government revealed in February 2021 that its officials were aware of wrongdoing for years and had failed to intervene (BBC).

cases.title: De Winter Commission — violence in Dutch youth care since 1945
cases.who: Dutch residential youth care, foster care, juvenile justice institutions, closed youth care, shelters for unaccompanied asylum-seeking minors, institutions for disabled children
cases.what: The commission led by Professor Micha de Winter published 'Onvoldoende beschermd' on 14 June 2019 after interviewing about 1,000 people who had lived in foster families or youth institutions. It found that a considerable share of children in Dutch youth care since 1945 were not adequately protected from physical, psychological and sexual violence, that supervisors did not intervene enough, and that the government did too little to prevent it. The cabinet said the violence 'should never have happened' and set up a payment scheme for victims.

cases.title: Netherlands — De Vries Commission on sexual abuse in organised sport (2017)
cases.who: Dutch sports clubs and federations; NOC*NSF
cases.what: The Dutch Olympic Committee NOC*NSF set up a commission led by former minister Klaas de Vries in May 2017; it reported on 12 December 2017. A survey found about 12% of athletes had experienced sexually transgressive behaviour as children and about 4% sexual assault or rape. The commission analysed 686 cases reported between 2001 and 2017, in which 60% of victims were under 16 and 70% of perpetrators were coaches or supervisors, and received 103 new reports. It recommended a reporting duty for sports boards.

cases.title: Deetman Commission — supplementary inquiry into abuse of and violence against girls in the Catholic Church (2013)
cases.who: Roman Catholic Church in the Netherlands — dioceses and religious orders
cases.what: The Deetman Commission presented a supplementary inquiry on 11 March 2013 into sexual abuse of and violence against girls and young women who were minors in the Dutch Catholic Church from 1945 to 2012, after its 2011 report had found over 77% of identified victims were male. It received 79 new reports, of which 37 concerned only physical or psychological violence, and reconsidered 71 earlier reports of violence, 26 from women. It called on bishops and religious superiors to reach out to these victims; reports involving sexual abuse go to the Church's reporting point and compensation committees.

cases.title: Deetman Commission — Catholic Church in the Netherlands
cases.who: Catholic dioceses and religious orders in the Netherlands
cases.what: The commission led by former minister Wim Deetman, set up by the church in March 2010, reported on 16 December 2011. It identified at least 800 priests, monks and other religious who abused children between 1945 and 1985, 105 of them still alive, and estimated tens of thousands of victims. It found bishops and officials knew of the abuse and followed a policy of avoiding scandal.
cases.cover_up: Policy of 'not hanging out the dirty washing'; bishops and officials knew and did not act

cases.title: Utrecht University / WODC study — Jehovah's Witnesses in the Netherlands
cases.who: Jehovah's Witnesses (Netherlands)
cases.what: A study by Utrecht University researchers led by Kees van den Bos, commissioned by the Ministry of Justice's research centre WODC, was published on 23 January 2020. 751 participants reported experiences; only 27% of cases led to a police report. Victims were critical of internal handling by elders; the researchers recommended better support, elder training, an internal reporting centre, and that lawmakers consider a duty to report abuse to police.

flows.title: Seoul → Netherlands
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Netherlands; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Colombo → Netherlands
flows.what: Sri Lankan babies adopted to the Netherlands in the 1980s, many through baby farms and falsified papers; others went to the UK, Sweden, Denmark and Germany.

flows.title: Athens → Netherlands
flows.what: Greek-born children adopted to Netherlands 1950–1975; Greece restored their citizenship by law on 2 May 2025.

flows.title: Buyers in 24 countries → Philippines (HSI data)
flows.what: Europol's 2024 sprint on US HSI data: chats between about 12,000 criminal customer accounts and 100 sellers in the Philippines; packages may lead 24 countries to 197 buyers. Origin point is The Hague (sprint host), not a buyer country.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in the Netherlands (IWF 2025)
flows.what: The Netherlands was the largest host of IWF-actioned material for years (47% in 2018); its share fell to 11% in 2025. INHOPE 2025 still ranks it first for confirmed CSAM (36%).

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Dreamboard
networks.what: Invitation-only board, about 600 members; 72 charged in Operation Delego (2011). Start year is approximate (investigation launched 2009).

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

networks.name: Boystown
networks.what: Tor platform with 400,000 registered users; four German administrators sentenced 7–12 years (2022).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.

networks.name: The Com
networks.what: Transnational network of online groups (incl. 764, CVLT) involved in sextortion, child sexual exploitation, swatting and other crimes; FBI public warning 23 July 2025; Europol Project COMPASS since 2025. Start year approximate.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2021: Panama — National Assembly subcommission and prosecutors on abuse in state-supervised shelters (2021).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

cases.title: Cartagena — 'La Madame' network exploiting girls for tourists (plea 2018)
cases.who: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ('La Madame')
cases.what: Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello ran a sex network from a Bocagrande apartment in Cartagena, supplying young women and minors to parties on yachts, in hotels and at beaches and sending women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas; prosecutors seized 15 ledgers of clients and payments, and a WhatsApp group listed 200 women. In 2018 she accepted charges of human trafficking and conspiracy in a plea deal and was sentenced to eight years and one month; she was released on parole in 2023. US ICE supported the investigation.
cases.cover_up: At hearings she threatened to reveal the names of politicians and powerful men she said were clients (her claim, unverified).

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Panama — legislative subcommission and prosecutors on abuse in state-supervised shelters
cases.who: Private and NGO shelters (albergues) under the Secretaría de Niñez, Adolescencia y Familia (Senniaf)
cases.what: A National Assembly subcommission report in early February 2021 found cases of abuse in shelters for children at social risk. By March 2021 the Public Ministry had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and identified 20 victims, who were moved; five people had been charged with offences including child mistreatment, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters inspected.
cases.cover_up: The Ombudsman found 70% of 44 shelters inspected lacked suitable staff and that Senniaf did little follow-up.

cases.title: Operación Roblox — extortion network in Panama
cases.who: A man in Puerto Caimito, La Chorrera (Panamá Oeste), arrested in 'Operación Roblox'
cases.what: On 23 October 2024 Panama's National Police and Public Ministry carried out 'Operación Roblox' in Puerto Caimito, La Chorrera district, arresting a man accused of illicit contact with minors through the Roblox gaming platform and of threatening them to demand child sexual abuse material. The alert came from Spanish police investigating a child sexual abuse material network; phones and laptops were seized and investigations were continuing.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: UN peacekeeping data, 2025 (SG report A/80/644): Few finalised: e.g. one Togolese officer — repatriation and 60 days' imprisonment; 'pending additional information from the member state'
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: South Sudan — 'sex for aid' allegations against aid workers, Malakal UN Protection of Civilians site.
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: Almost no reports reach the international systems
patterns.role_note: NCMEC 2025: 863 reports for South Sudan
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Lord's Resistance Army — child abduction and sexual slavery; ICC conviction of Dominic Ongwen
cases.who: Lord's Resistance Army (LRA), leader Joseph Kony (ICC warrant outstanding)
cases.what: The LRA abducted tens of thousands of children in northern Uganda for use as fighters, porters and 'wives'; UNICEF estimated at least 25,000 by 2006. On 4 February 2021 ICC Trial Chamber IX convicted Sinia Brigade commander Dominic Ongwen, himself abducted as a child, of 61 crimes including rape, sexual slavery, forced marriage, forced pregnancy and the conscription and use of children under 15 (2002–2005); he was sentenced to 25 years on 6 May 2021, confirmed on appeal 15 December 2022. From 2008 the LRA abducted thousands more in DR Congo, South Sudan and CAR.

cases.title: South Sudan — sexual violence against girls by SSPDF and other forces (UN verified)
cases.who: South Sudan People's Defence Forces (SSPDF), SPLM/A-IO factions, police
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 94 girls, as young as 7, in South Sudan in 2022, 74 of them by the South Sudan People's Defence Forces, plus SPLM/A-IO Kit-Gwang (10), SPLM/A-IO (4) and the National Police Service (2). In 2024 it verified sexual violence against 7 girls, 5 by the SSPDF.

cases.title: UN — Secretary-General's annual SEA reports: 27 child victims in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024
cases.who: UN peacekeepers, civilian staff, agency staff and implementing partners
cases.what: The Secretary-General reports each year to the General Assembly on special measures for protection from sexual exploitation and abuse. The report released in March 2025 recorded 102 allegations in peacekeeping and political missions in 2024, 44 in DR Congo and 40 in the Central African Republic, with 125 victims, 27 of them children; there were also 190 allegations against staff of UN agencies, funds and programmes and 382 against staff of implementing partners. The supplementary tables list child victims in MINUSCA (Central African Republic, 13), MONUSCO (DR Congo, 9), UNMISS (South Sudan, 2), UNMIL (Liberia, 2) and UNITAD (Iraq, 1). It noted about 750 paternity claims involving peacekeepers since 2006, more than 500 still pending.
cases.cover_up: About 750 paternity and child support claims against peacekeeping personnel since 2006, more than 500 still pending; claims are referred to troop-contributing countries, most of which have not taken meaningful action

cases.title: South Sudan — UN Commission finds rape, abduction and sexual slavery of women and girls by armed forces and groups (2022)
cases.who: South Sudan People's Defence Forces, opposition forces and armed groups; intercommunal militias
cases.what: The UN Commission on Human Rights in South Sudan presented a report on conflict-related sexual violence to the Human Rights Council on 18 March 2022. It found that parties to the conflict used rape of women and girls as a weapon of terror and political repression, and that abductions of women and girls for forced marriage and sexual slavery had increased in Jonglei, the Greater Pibor Administrative Area, Warrap and Lakes. It noted that a military court in Yei had convicted SSPDF soldiers of rape in late 2020 but victims had not been paid court-ordered compensation.
cases.cover_up: Commission described impunity for armed forces in Western Equatoria; court-ordered compensation to victims in Yei unpaid

cases.title: South Sudan — 'sex for aid' allegations against aid workers, Malakal UN Protection of Civilians site
cases.who: Staff named from IOM, MSF, WFP, World Vision and others in a UN-run camp
cases.what: A September 2022 investigation by The New Humanitarian and Al Jazeera reported that between 2015 and 2022 aid workers in the UN-run Malakal Protection of Civilians site exploited displaced women and girls, including 'sex for aid'; women and girls reported being raped and becoming pregnant. Staff of IOM, MSF, WFP and World Vision were among those named.

networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. patterns.pattern: Years of waiting: protected by status
patterns.role_note: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo: first report 2019, first action 2022 (3 years). Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them
patterns.pattern_summary: For 41 cases on this map the sources give two dates: the year a complaint first reached the police, a church, an employer or another official body, and the year someone was first charged, convicted or named in an official finding. The middle of those waits is 12 years. In Rochdale in 1968, a pupil told the police about the local politician Cyril Smith and was told that Smith was "a very important, powerful man". In 1970 Smith was assured he would not be prosecuted. In 2012, two years after his death, prosecutors said he should have been charged. Complaints about Jimmy Savile, one of the BBC's best-known presenters, reached the police from 1958, and he was never charged while he was alive. Gymnasts complained about the team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997, and he was first charged in 2016. The map colors each country by the longest wait among its cases.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2005: Timor-Leste — CAVR 'Chega!' report on children removed to Indonesia (2005).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Timor-Leste — Truth commission finds over 4,000 children taken to Indonesia, renamed and converted (2005).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Richard Daschbach — Topu Honis shelter, Oecusse
cases.who: Society of the Divine Word (SVD); US-born Fr Richard Daschbach
cases.what: US-born Divine Word missionary Richard Daschbach founded the Topu Honis children's shelter in Oecusse in 1992. After a complaint to his superiors in February 2018 he admitted the abuse to them in March 2018, and the Vatican dismissed him from the priesthood on 6 November 2018; the church did not tell the public. He was arrested in April 2019 and charged with 14 counts of sexually abusing children under 14, plus child abuse material and domestic violence counts. On 21 December 2021 a court in Oecusse sentenced him to 12 years, basing the verdict on the testimony of four victims. A report by the Dili archdiocese's Justice and Peace Commission had defended him.

cases.title: Timor-Leste — Truth commission finds over 4,000 children taken to Indonesia, renamed and converted (2005)
cases.who: Indonesian military; Islamic and other organisations and individuals that took children
cases.what: The Commission for Reception, Truth and Reconciliation (CAVR) published its final report, Chega!, in 2005, covering 1974 to 1999. It found that at least 4,000 children were forcibly taken from their families and moved illegally to Indonesia during the occupation, by military units, some of which used them as child soldiers or servants, and by Islamic organisations that converted them; children were often renamed and lost contact with their families. It called separating a child from their true identity, culture, religion or language a grave breach of the Fourth Geneva Convention. CAVR and the joint Indonesia–Timor-Leste Commission of Truth and Friendship recommended a commission to search for the missing children, which was never created.

cases.title: Bishop Carlos Ximenes Belo — Vatican sanctions
cases.who: Salesians; Bishop Carlos Filipe Ximenes Belo (Nobel Peace laureate)
cases.what: On 28 September 2022 Dutch magazine De Groene Amsterdammer reported that two men said Bishop Belo had abused them and other boys in Fatumaca and Dili, before and during his time as bishop. The next day the Vatican confirmed it had received allegations in 2019 and imposed disciplinary sanctions in 2020: limits on movement and ministry, no contact with minors and no contact with Timor-Leste. The sanctions were reinforced in 2021. Belo had left Timor in 2002 and worked in Maputo, Mozambique from 2004.
cases.cover_up: Vatican received allegations in 2019 and imposed sanctions in 2020 but did not disclose them until a magazine reported the case in 2022

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

networks.name: Salesians of Don Bosco
networks.what: Order present in more than 130 countries. Documented cases include Boys' Town Sydney, the Don Rua juvenate in the Netherlands, US schools, Julian Fox (moved from Australia to Fiji in 1999), and Vatican sanctions on Salesian Bishop Belo of Timor-Leste.

cases.title: Yemen — sexual violence against children by government-affiliated forces and Houthis (UN verified)
cases.who: Yemen Armed Forces and affiliated forces (police, Security Belt, Amaliqah); Houthis
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 24 children (8 boys, 16 girls) in Yemen in 2023, 20 attributed to the Yemen Armed Forces and affiliated forces (Yemen Armed Forces 9, Yemeni police 4). In 2024 it verified 11 cases (6 boys, 5 girls), attributed to the Houthis (2), Yemen Armed Forces (2) and affiliated forces (7), including Yemeni police (4).

cases.title: Yemen — UN Group of Eminent Experts: rape of boys and girls by armed forces; sexual violence against recruited girls
cases.who: Security Belt Forces; Yemeni 35th Armoured Brigade; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa; Houthi de facto authorities
cases.what: The Group of Eminent Experts on Yemen, mandated by the UN Human Rights Council, reported in September 2019 (A/HRC/42/17) that Security Belt Forces raped 18 women, four boys and a girl in 2016–2019 and committed widespread rape of migrant women, girls and boys at a former facility in Aden; members of the 35th Armoured Brigade raped two boys; UAE personnel at Al-Bureiqa raped a boy; and Houthi detention sites saw sexual violence against a 17-year-old boy. Its September 2020 report found credible accounts that the Houthis recruited 34 girls aged 13–17 between June 2015 and June 2020, 12 of whom reportedly suffered sexual violence, forced early marriage linked to recruitment, or both. The Group said its figures were a small sample.
